passages.t: A ruined loincloth and filled wineskins
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth and wear it, but not to let it touch water (verse 1). Then he tells him to take it to Perath and hide it in a crevice of the rocks (verse 4). Many days later Jeremiah goes back and digs it up. ‘But now it was ruined’ (verse 7), of no use at all.

‘In the same way I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem’ (verse 9). These people refuse to listen and follow the stubbornness of their hearts and other gods (verse 10). ‘For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s waist, so I have made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to Me’ (verse 11), to be his people, his fame, praise and glory. But they would not listen.

Then a saying: every wineskin will be filled with wine. The people will answer that everyone knows that (verse 12). But God means he will fill everyone in the land with drunkenness, from the kings on David's throne to the priests and prophets (verse 13), and smash them against one another (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
A loincloth was the garment worn closest to the body, wrapped round the hips. Linen was the material of priestly clothing, so it may hint at Israel's calling to be a priestly people. The point God draws is closeness: Israel was meant to cling to God as that garment clings to a man.

Where Perath was is debated. The Hebrew word is the usual name for the Euphrates, roughly 350 miles from Jerusalem, which would make Jeremiah's two trips a matter of months. Others note a village called Parah in Benjamin, a few miles from Anathoth, whose name sounds like the river's. On either reading, the hidden garment rots near the waters of Babylon, the place of exile.

The wineskin saying was a common proverb, the sort of thing everyone agrees with. Jeremiah turns it into a picture of a people made drunk and helpless, crashing into each other.
passages.later: Moses said God chose Israel ‘to be a people for His prized possession’ (Deuteronomy 7:6). Isaiah pictures the same drunkenness of judgment: ‘stagger, but not from strong drink’ (Isaiah 29:9).
passages.asks: God made his people to cling to him, and they rotted away from him. Ask what it means for you to cling to God as closely as clothing. And ask what pride in you might need to be ruined so you can be close to him again.

passages.t: Give glory before the darkness, and can the leopard change his spots?
passages.happening:
‘Listen and give heed. Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken’ (verse 15). ‘Give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness’ (verse 16), before their feet stumble on the darkening hills. If they will not listen, Jeremiah will weep in secret because of their pride, for the LORD's flock has been taken captive (verse 17).

The king and the queen mother are told to take a lowly seat, ‘for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads’ (verse 18). The towns of the Negev are shut, and all Judah is carried into exile (verse 19). Jerusalem is asked where the flock is that was entrusted to her (verse 20). The allies she trained will rule over her, and pain will grip her like a woman in labor (verse 21).

If she asks why this has happened, it is because of her great iniquity that she has been shamed (verse 22). ‘Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?’ (verse 23). No more can those used to doing evil learn to do good (verse 23). God will scatter them like chaff (verse 24), because they forgot him and trusted in falsehood (verse 25). He has seen their idolatry on the hills (verse 27). ‘How long will you remain unclean?’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Most interpreters take the king and queen mother as Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta. He came to the throne at eighteen, reigned three months, and surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC, when he, his mother and his officials were taken to Babylon. The queen mother held a recognized office in Judah, and the books of Kings name the mother of nearly every king.

The Negev was the dry south of Judah. If its towns were shut, the land was closed off from the south as well as the north.

Verse 23 is a proverb about what cannot be changed by one's own effort. A leopard cannot remove its spots, nor anyone their own skin. The proverb uses a people's skin as one of two things that do not change; it makes no judgment on the Ethiopians, and it gives no warrant for any prejudice. Its target is Judah's habit of evil, so set that it could not be undone from within.
passages.later: Jehoiachin's surrender is told in Kings: ‘Jehoiachin king of Judah, his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials all surrendered to the king of Babylon’ (2 Kings 24:12). Ezekiel promises what Judah could not do for itself: ‘I will give you a new heart’ (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.hard:
Verses 22 and 26 picture Jerusalem as a woman stripped and shamed. How should a reader take that?

The prophets pictured Jerusalem as God's wife and her idolatry as adultery, and they drew on the ancient practice of shaming an unfaithful woman and on the real horrors armies inflicted on captured cities. Some scholars argue that the picture reflects and risks reinforcing violence against women and must be read critically. Others stress that the figure is a city and its leaders, who were men, and that the picture is meant to shock the men in power by casting them as the disgraced party. Both can be true. The same book pictures God as a husband longing to take his bride back (3:12-14; 31:3-4).

This is a prophetic picture of a city and a covenant. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm any woman.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The leopard cannot change his spots, and Judah could not change itself. Ask what habit in you seems impossible to change by your own effort. And ask what it would mean to give glory to God now, before the darkness comes.
